He rammed it in with a sharp jerk, enough to make the wood groan, then chipped at the edges with the jagged end, carving out a wider gap. “You better have something useful in you,” he breathed, voice low and harsh. He slammed the rail back into the drawer seam and heaved sideways, the wood groaning against the pressure. “Come on, come on...” Another shock lit up the air. He felt it before he heard it — the air shifted, like it had been pulled taut and then slapped. The static crackled through the walls. It hit something metal hard enough that Jake could hear the furniture rattle. Leon’s scream followed a heartbeat later. Brief. Only half-formed. It cut out partway, leaving a silence so sharp it felt surgical. Jake swore under his breath, twisting the rail like a crowbar. The wood groaned, splintered, and snapped — a sliver of lacquered veneer shooting up and nearly clipped his cheek. The drawer shifted. He froze. Then yanked. Chapter 5: Tarnished Steel The drawer gave way with a cracking snap — Too loud. Far too loud for a building where silence was the only safe currency left. Jake flinched, jaw clenching as the sound echoed out through the sterile quiet. He stilled, one hand still frozen against the wood, ears straining for the rhythm of boots on tile or the flicker of static bleed in the air. Nothing. Yet. He exhaled carefully through his nose, fingers tightening on the warped handle. Planting a foot against the base of the desk, he pulled again, bracing his weight into it. The splintered wood protested with a dull groan as it scraped against the twisted bracket still trying, uselessly, to hold the drawer shut. The makeshift crowbar — a bent chunk of railing he’d scavenged from the stairwell — slipped from his grip and hit the floor with a metallic clatter. Jake didn’t wait for the echo to fade. He shoved his hands into the gap and ripped , the drawer tearing free with a final shudder, fragments of lacquered wood shearing off under his fingers. He dug in fast — no time for care, no thought spared for preservation. Just fingers tearing through decades of damp files and soot-stained paper, old notes soaked through and curling at the edges. Pages dissolved under his touch, mold blooming like bruises across forgotten ink. The drawer vomited its contents to the floor — a mess of shredded vellum, crumbling edges, the occasional splash of something he didn’t want to name. A few metal implements rolled free: surgical scissors dulled to uselessness, an old spoon warped into a lazy curl, a leather strap whose cracked buckles were flecked with something dry and reddish that he told himself — firmly — was rust. He shoved it all aside. And there — barely visible, half-tucked beneath a square of stiff cloth — a glint. Jake fished it out carefully. A key. His breath caught. Then another glint. A second. They were handcuff keys. A pair of them. So much smaller than he thought they would be, thin, clearly designed to fit only one kind of lock. And rusted. Deep-set corrosion traced along the edge of the first one like veins. The second looked slightly better, but it, too, was tarnished — a dull, almost green-tinged patina marring the pin. They looked entirely too fragile to be of use; the corruption of the Entity having clearly sunk deep into the metal just like everything else that might have once been useful. Jake stared at them, a cold pit forming in his gut. “...Fuck.” He rubbed one hard against his shirt, trying to clear the buildup, but the oxidation flaked like scabs, and underneath was just more of the same. He thought briefly about trying to chip the buildup off against something, then rejected it. The moment the thought had arrived, so did the vision of the key snapping in the cuff, leaving Leon trapped with a broken stem and no second chance. No. They might work. Maybe. If he was careful. And lucky. He didn’t have time to doubt. Jake turned, keys in hand — and stopped. The lights overhead twitched , the fluorescents stuttering like a skipped heartbeat. The air flexed , pressure building in the doorframe behind him, and with a soft whine like a rising scream, the hallway bathed in red. No time. He bolted. The nearest window frame was half-splintered already, and he threw himself through it in one motion — boots clipping the wood, arm up to guard his head — and tumbled into the hall beyond in a skidding roll. The hallway was already hissing when he hit the corner — the air charged, laced with static that prickled down his spine like pins. Behind him, the air screamed with a high frequency whine, coupled with the heavy boot-falls of something significantly larger than him, moving at great pace. Herman had definitely heard the drawer break. Jake didn’t look back. He couldn’t afford to. A burst of static ripped through the corridor behind him, snapping off a nearby panel and detonating against the floor just out of reach. Sparks skittered across the tiles, hot enough that he felt the heat on his shins. His feet skidded. Momentum stole his balance for a second — then he caught himself, twisting hard as he slammed shoulder-first into the next corner and careened down a new hallway. One of the keys flicked out of his grip mid-turn, bounced once, and slid across the linoleum with a traitorous rattle. “Shit—!” He spun out wide, snatched it back up in a near dive, and didn’t pause to check for damage. The seconds were bleeding . He needed to lose him. Somehow. Loop a vault. Take a back route. Anything. But Léry’s didn’t offer clean chase paths.
